articles.title: Bryson DeChambeau speaks out for first time since LIV Golf shutdown, reveals immediate plans for December
articles.summary: In his first public statement since LIV Golf announced its shutdown, Bryson DeChambeau reflects on his time with the league and discusses his upcoming participation in the Nedbank Golf Challenge in December, while leaving his long-term plans open-ended amid critical deadlines for joining established tours.
articles.body: Bryson DeChambeau has spoken publicly for the first time since LIV Golf confirmed it would wind down operations, reflecting on his four years with the Saudi-backed league while leaving his own future unresolved. The two-time US Open champion stopped short of confirming whether he intends to return to the PGA Tour or join the DP World Tour, with a key membership deadline approaching.DeChambeau reflects on four years with LIV GolfDeChambeau joined LIV Golf in 2022, becoming one of the most prominent players to leave the established professional circuit for the breakaway league. His decision came during a period of significant upheaval in men's golf, when players including Brooks Koepka, Dustin Johnson and Phil Mickelson also accepted reported eight- and nine-figure contracts to join the Saudi-backed competition.The defections triggered a prolonged dispute between LIV Golf and the established tours. The PGA Tour and European Tour initially imposed restrictions on players who had joined the breakaway circuit, although some of those rules have since been relaxed.Following LIV Golf's announcement that it would cease operations, DeChambeau issued a statement reflecting on his time with the league without expressing regret over his decision.“I’m not going to rewrite the past four years,” he said.“I made a decision I believed in, and I’m grateful for what came with it: playing in front of fans new and old around the world who rarely got to see the best players at home.”He singled out Adelaide in Australia and Johannesburg in South Africa among the destinations that made a lasting impression during his time with LIV Golf.The American also defended the league's team format, which he believes remains a worthwhile concept even if its future structure changes. LIV Golf's tournaments featured 57 players divided into 13 teams, with separate individual and team competitions, before the season concluded with a bracket-style team championship involving singles and alternate-shot matches.“I still believe in team golf,” DeChambeau said. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.”He added that he had given everything he could to make the format work during his time with the league.What happens next for DeChambeau?While DeChambeau made clear that his commitment to growing the sport remains unchanged, he offered no confirmation about where he intends to compete once LIV Golf shuts down.His immediate schedule includes the Nedbank Golf Challenge in December, Gary Player's tournament in South Africa. DeChambeau said he was looking forward to returning after the reception he received during his first visit to the country.“In December, I’ll compete at the Nedbank Golf Challenge, Gary Player’s event, in front of fans who made my first visit to South Africa unforgettable. Beyond that, I’ll go about whatever is next the right way,” he said.“My passion is to grow this game. That’s still the goal. Thank you for sticking with me. Together we can grow this great game we all love.”The question of his longer-term future remains significant because DeChambeau has until November 15 to declare his intention to become a member of the DP World Tour. Missing that deadline could leave him without a straightforward route back into the established professional circuits, potentially limiting his opportunities beyond the major championships.DeChambeau is among the most recognisable figures in modern golf, with nine PGA Tour victories and two US Open titles. He won his first major at Winged Foot in 2020 before claiming a second at Pinehurst in 2024.LIV Golf's shutdown followed the withdrawal of financial backing from Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. The league had been unable to secure the additional investment required to proceed with its proposed LIV 2.0 plans for 2027, and confirmed in US bankruptcy court on Thursday that it would wind down operations.For DeChambeau, the immediate commitment is South Africa. What follows will depend on the decisions he makes as the breakaway league's players begin considering their next steps.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Welcome to college football's new reality: Make the 24-team playoff or get fired
articles.summary: Will more playoff access really calm down the "Fire Everyone" culture in college football? Here's a prediction: It'll make it far, far worse.
articles.body:
As support grew for the College Football Playoff to expand from 12 to 24 teams, money was not the primary factor.

Yes, the new five-year, $1.7 billion deal finalized Monday will add a few million for each school in the SEC and Big Ten and a smaller amount for everyone else. But replacing conference championship games with a bunch of first-round playoff games was not, on its own, a big enough pot of gold to blow up the entire sport and risk losing the sanctity of the regular season.

What was worth it? Access. As coaches and administrators experienced the 12-team playoff, they came to the conclusion — and probably correctly — that nothing resonates with fans anymore besides getting into the field. They increasingly saw their own job security tied to the black-and-white standard of being in or out, so they simply changed the standard to include far more programs stuck in the middle of the two richest conferences.

But will more playoff access really calm down the "Fire Everyone" culture that seems to be increasingly pervasive in college football? Here's a prediction: It'll make it far, far worse.

Though it was a slow start to this year's coaching carousel, business is picking up with four power conference openings and several more that could materialize in the coming weeks. The real surprise, though, is how many first-year coaches are already under pressure.

Michigan's Kyle Whittingham, California's Tosh Lupoi, Washington State's Kirby Moore, Colorado State's Jim Mora and Tulane's Will Hall have been so disappointing in Year 1 that it wouldn't be a shock if their schools pulled the plug and started over. Even at places like Arkansas and Florida, where the record is no different from what was expected, first-year coaches are struggling to convince fans they are on the right track.

Traditionally, firing a coach after one year was taboo unless there was an off-field scandal. Even if it was immediately clear to university administrators that they hired a coach who was in over his head, it was almost too embarrassing to admit such a mistake without at least two years of on-field evidence.

But if that culture is indeed changing and compressing the timeline for coaches to prove themselves, the 24-team playoff is going to be like dumping kerosene on a bonfire.

If you thought the 12-team playoff created a world of FOMO for everyone who didn't get in, just wait until two-thirds of the power conference schools realize every November that they landed on the wrong side of a pass-fail test.

When the standard is really, really high to make the playoff, you can at least rationalize not making it. Even now, in the 12-team version, we have seen good teams like Texas, Notre Dame and Vanderbilt last year all fall short because there wasn't enough room and the margin for error was small. If you fell short of the cut line, you were in good company.

So when you change the threshold so dramatically, you are of course including more teams worthy of a shot. But you are also creating a new standard for what constitutes a successful season. It's inevitable that, starting next year, fans and boosters will consume college football in a much more binary fashion: You're either in or you're out, and it's a big problem if you're out.

At the same time, college football is undergoing an Overton window revolution on what kind of season is acceptable for a new coach. It used to be, the first year was a free pass. Especially at programs that had lost for a few years, the results didn't matter. All you had to do was show that you've changed the locker room culture, be a little bit more competitive than the last coach, and secure a good recruiting class to keep fans happy.

Those days are gone. Even if Curt Cignetti getting Indiana to the playoff in Year 1 and winning a national title in Year 2 is the extreme example, he's far from alone in using the transfer portal to engineer an immediate turnaround. When fans see Bob Chesney get UCLA to 9-0, Will Stein put Kentucky into the CFP mix, Eric Morris win quickly at Oklahoma State with players he coached at North Texas and James Franklin put the best Virginia Tech team on the field in nearly a decade, everyone has a right to ask, "Why not us?"

If you're trying to figure out what's fueling so much anger right now at a place like Florida, which is 5-4 and has not been bad overall in Jon Sumrall's first year, look no further. Under a traditional timeline, Florida fans would generally be in agreement that Sumrall needs time to rebuild the program after five straight mediocre (or worse) seasons and wouldn't start rendering any judgments until Year 3.

But now that it's proven you can flip any program in a year, that becomes the expectation. Nobody can afford to play the long game anymore. At 5-4 with wins over Texas and Ole Miss, Sumrall is not on the hot seat and has largely been fine. But will the chatter about his job security move from the online world to the real world if he's not on track to make the 24-team playoff at this time next year?

The collision of those two factors — expanding the playoff and the recent track record of coaches winning in Year 1 — will inevitably accelerate all the conversations fans are having when they start to wonder if they've got the right guy. And as we see around the country every year, prohibitive finances are no match for administrative self-preservation.

For weeks, Florida State officials were adamant that they wanted to bring back Mike Norvell, largely because his approximate $50 million buyout was such an issue. When the noise got loud enough, though, the school president caved. We could see the same thing starting to unfold at Nebraska, where Matt Rhule signed a new contract last year with a $63 million buyout but now finds himself at the center of a fan mutiny after losing four straight.

These are not healthy developments, but Newton's Third Law of Motion always wins in the end. For every action (massive coaching contracts, playoff expansion, transfer portal free-for-all), there will be an equal and opposite reaction (new expectations, more pressure, less patience to build from the ground up). The old rules no longer apply.

But there is a real problem with what they've done here. At 24 teams, there are still going to be more losers than winners at the end of every college football season; only now, it will make the line between the two that much brighter. Everyone will feel that much more pressure to be on the right side of the divide because it will be viewed as unacceptable to fall short.

There are plenty of reasons why expanding the playoff makes sense. Increased parity means more than 12 teams deserve a chance, donors are being asked to pour $40-50 million into rosters without enough postseason rewards and there was no way to rescue the bowl system given all the focus on the CFP. The conference championship games had also gotten stale since realignment helped form 16- and 18-team mega-conferences, so there is some logic in replacing them with first-round playoff games.

But if coaches and administrators think that a team squeaking into the playoff as the No. 22 seed will spare them from the "Fire Everyone" culture they seek to tame, it will prove to be a delusion. And if God forbid they miss the 24-team playoff, they will soon get a lesson in unintended consequences.

articles.title: Manchester United's Michael Carrick Expected to Be Fired as Manager, New Rumors Link Pochettino
articles.summary: Change is coming to Manchester United.
articles.body:
According to David Ornstein, Adam Crafton and Laurie Whitwell of The Athletic , the club is "expected to relieve" manager Michael Carrick of his duties.

Per that report, "The club continue to insist that no decision has been reached but multiple sources, speaking to The Athletic on the condition of anonymity to protect relationships, indicate work has been undertaken on potential replacements and the anticipation is a change will be made before the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool in 13 days' time."

USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino is reportedly considered a candidate, although Manchester United would have to trigger his $10 million buyout clause, per Paul Tenorio, Tom Bogert and Henry Bushnell of The Athletic .

Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann also reportedly "have admirers at the club," per Ornstein, Crafton and Whitwell.

Carrick, 45, replaced Ruben Amorim in January on an interim basis and was appointed to the full-time gig in May after leading United to 11 wins across 16 matches, with the club finishing third on the Premier League table and earning a berth in the Champions League.

But the 2026-27 campaign has been an abject disaster. Manchester United currently sit 18th on the table with just eight points through 10 matches, a stunning run of mediocrity for the proud club.

Manchester United have had a revolving door of managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, with 11 different men holding the gig as caretakers or on a full-time basis. The Red Devils haven't won a Premier League title in that time, which has also coincided with the unpopular ownership of the Glazer family (Jim Ratcliffe leading football operations was supposed to help in that regard, though the returns to this point haven't been promising).

The constant turnover at manager, paired with inconsistent approaches to roster-building and a general sense of dysfunction within the club have led to a sustained period of United finding themselves trailing far behind Premier League powers like Arsenal, Liverpool, Chelsea and Manchester City (115 charges notwithstanding) over the past two decades.

That's the context the next manager will have to shoulder as he hopes to right the ship.

articles.title: USMNT coach Mauricio Pochettino reportedly among top candidates to join Manchester United if Michael Carrick is fired
articles.summary: Pochettino signed an extension this summer to stay with the U.S. through the 2030 World Cup, but that contract reportedly includes a $10 million release clau...
articles.body:
With Manchester United in dire straits, the English club might be looking to United States men's national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino as a potential new leader. Pochettino has emerged as one of the favored candidates to succeed United manager Michael Carrick if he is fired, ESPN reported Monday .

United is currently third-to-last in the Premier League table and facing relegation for the first time since the division was created. Carrick has spent the season on the hot seat, but is on the brink of finally being sacked after failing to turn the season around.

ESPN reports that discussions on whether to fire Carrick are still ongoing, but there is a sense of "acceptance" that a new manager is needed.

Candidates that are reportedly being considered include former Newcastle coach Eddie Howe, former Germany manager Julian Nagelsmann and former Ipswich Town head coach Kieran McKenna, per ESPN. But Pochettino, who coached at Tottenham, PSG and Chelsea before taking the USMNT job in 2024, has reportedly emerged as a frontrunner.

Pochettino agreed to stay with the USMNT on a new contract in early August, with the deal keeping the 54-year-old Argentine in charge of the Stars and Stripes through the 2030 World Cup. Coming off its best World Cup performance in decades, the move was intended to give the U.S. some continuity for the next four-year World Cup cycle.

ESPN reports that Pochettino's contract includes a $10 million release clause, which Man United would have to pay in order to hire Pochettino.

Manchester United started the 2026-27 Premier League season with a stunning 2-0 loss to recently promoted Hull City. Things have not gotten much better for the team since then, with highlights including a derby loss to a short-handed Manchester City and a crumbling 2-0 loss to Chelsea last week.

The Red Devils currently have only one win across the first 10 games of the season, and are one point out of last place in the Premier League.

Pochettino has expressed an interest in embracing a "fresh start" for the next cycle, and has utilized the country's young up-and-coming players in recent international breaks. However, Pochettino's departure would leave the USMNT without that sense of direction, though with plenty of time to find a new coach before the next World Cup.

articles.title: La nueva vida de éxitos de Vozinha no se detiene tras el Mundial
articles.standfirst: Vozinha (40 años) da la vuelta olímpica en Chile en festejo de Colo Colo en el Monumental
articles.summary: Vozinha (40 años) da la vuelta olímpica en Chile en festejo de Colo Colo en el Monumental
articles.body: El mediático portero mundialista de Cabo Verde Josimar José Évora Dias 'Vozinha' celebró en Chile el título conseguido con Colo Colo, dando la vuelta olímpica junto al plantel en el festejo por la estrella 35 del club realizado en el estadio Monumental de Santiago. El Cacique se coronó campeón de la liga chilena tras vencer -2 en su visita a Ñublense, consolidando una ventaja irremontable de 10 puntos frente a la Universidad de Chile, cuando restan tres fechas para el final del campeonato. El guardameta, de 40 años, alzó la copa y fue ovacionado por la numerosa afición en las tribunas, tras haber sido clave en el duelo consagratorio al detener un remate en la última jugada, que pudo significar el empate rival. El jugador africano, sin embargo, no cobró protagonismo en los discursos de celebración en los que el ídolo albo Arturo Vidal tomó el micrófono para cantar con la hinchada mensajes contra su archirrival, la U. "El chuncho no lo puede creer, Colo Colo es lo más grande", dijo en referencia al conjunto universitario cuyo último título local fue en 2017. 'El King' jugó con los hinchas dejándoles el cierre de una frase que remató con una grosería: "Eso de ser campeones lo llevamos en la sangre y tienen que aceptarlo, chuncho conch...". Parte del plantel, cuerpo técnico y la directiva lucieron durante la celebración unos gorros tejidos llamados chilotes, que es una prenda de abrigo tradicional que tiene forma cónica y es originaria del sur de Chile, de donde es oriundo el presidente del club, Aníbal Mosa, quien lo usó de amuleto en la temporada. Fue precisamente Mosa quien informó, en medio del festejo, que el club ha iniciado las conversaciones para la renovación el entrenador argentino Fernando Ortiz, cuyo contrato vence en diciembre. "Está cerca de renovar, pero lo importante son los deseos y ganas, que el proyecto seduzca y una chispeza (astucia) que nos una para lograr cosas", dijo en la transmisión oficial en TNT Sports. Además del técnico, están pendientes otros acuerdos importantes como el de Vidal, quien en la previa dijo que "si Colo Colo fuera de la gente jugaría gratis, pero no es de la gente". Al respecto Mosa aclaró que luego de tener concretado el vínculo de Ortiz procederán con la plantilla, entre ellos 'Vozinha', quien también tiene un contrato que vence el próximo mes. El guardameta caboverdiano tiene una cláusula de extensión automática si disputa al menos el 50 % de los minutos que juegue el equipo en el período establecido en el acuerdo, una cuota que cumplirá si juega completo en dos partidos de los cinco que le restan a los albos y al menos 45 minutos más en otro.

articles.title: Bayern Munich midfielder Aleksandar Pavlović ‘delighted’ for Lennart Karl’s redemption
articles.summary: FC Bayern’s starlet is hustling and bustling to prove a point
articles.body:
Lennart Karl started the season in terrible form and was in the crosshairs of every single Bayern Munich fan, but the 18-year-old appears to have turned a corner with decent performances against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League and now a hard-fought 2-1 win against Mainz.

"I think, as a professional footballer, you simply have to be able to deal with things like that," Karl's teammate Aleksandar Pavlović said after the Mainz game (via @iMiaSanMia ). "I don't think he pays too much attention to what's going on outside. He just gets on with things and plays his football. I'm obviously delighted that he scored today as well."

Despite being undefeated this season so far, Bayern has not been playing at its highest level. This is a time when the team must rally together and put in a shift to get results. For Karl, he's done exactly that and wants to remind us why he was the breakout star of last season for Bayern.

articles.title: Everything Dan Lanning said before Oregon hosts Michigan
articles.summary: Dan Lanning looked back at Oregon's win over Ohio State and previewed the Ducks' matchup vs. Michigan at his weekly press conference.
articles.body:
The Oregon Ducks are riding high off back-to-back wins over ranked opponents and are suddenly back in the hunt for spots in both the Big Ten title game and the College Football Playoff. However, the Ducks will need to avoid a letdown at home this week against the Michigan Wolverines .

Dan Lanning has the Oregon offense rolling with Jay Johnson as the play-caller, and Dylan Raiola's steady play and downfield aggressiveness have given the Ducks a chance to finish the season strong and sneak into the playoff field. A 41-28 victory on the road over Ohio State was the last major hurdle for the Ducks to clear, but the Wolverines have made changes this week in anticipation of a trip to Eugene.

Coming off a 15-6 loss at home to Michigan State, Michigan fired offensive coordinator Jason Beck and reopened the quarterback competition in Ann Arbor between Bryce Underwood and Tommy Carr. The Wolverines' offense has been inept all season long, but some changes this week could make it a challenge to prepare for.

Oregon and Michigan have both played well defensively in recent weeks, meaning possessions and points could be at a premium on Saturday at Autzen Stadium. At his weekly press conference on Monday night, Lanning looked back on the win at Ohio State, addressed key injuries the Ducks are dealing with, and previewed this weekend's matchup with the Wolverines. Here is everything Lanning had to say before the Ducks host Michigan:

Dan Lanning: "Fun game there in Columbus. Obviously had some ebbs and flows, but really got on a heater with our players and, I think, saw some of the things we're capable of doing as a team. Just challenged our team that I want to see that team continue to grow, but there were some versions of us that were the best versions of us on Saturday. Fun thing to be a part of. Our guys came back and attacked at work today. (We are) about to play a Michigan team that's had some struggles, but you also see some unbelievable personnel. We've had the opportunity to go against coach Whittingham before and see where they really show up. They've always been tough-nosed. You see physicality. Obviously, their defense is probably as good as any defense that we played this season. They're playing really, really well. They've done some good things on special teams, and yes, they've had some struggles on offense, obviously, and recently had the coordinator change, but you do see a lot of talent over there. You see some talent on the offensive line. You see skill positions that can do things, and you see some quarterbacks that present different challenges. So this will be a fun prep week for us, a great opportunity to get our fans back in Autzen Stadium and get to experience that atmosphere and let them know what playing at Autzen is all about. We haven't had Michigan here at Autzen since we joined the Big Ten, so this will be a fun experience for us, especially with the rivalries and the opportunities that get created by being in this conference. So excited for it, and our guys are prepping hard to go to work."

Question: "You kind of alluded to it, some stretches in that game where you really looked like a great version of yourselves. Also a couple of potential turnovers they might have come up with that could have swung things. How do you feel like guys have balanced the last couple days, appreciating that you continue to show some growth the last couple weeks, while also knowing there's still more to be had?"

DL: "Yeah, I think it's just that you're really open and honest and point out exactly the reality of, 'OK, this went really well. Why did it go really well? This didn't go well.' There were plays that were called multiple times in the game; one time it's a touchdown, one time it's a tackle for loss on offense. Same thing with defenses that are called in the game, but I really do feel like a lot of our mindset going into that game was just do your job. When our guys went out there and did their job, they did it at a really high level and looked as good as any team in the country."

Q: "You guys were really good on third-and-long in this game. Conversely, you struggled on first down, especially running the ball. Is that scheme? Is it execution? What can you do better to not get behind the chains so much on first down?"

DL: "Yeah, I think that's something for us to certainly look at and attack. Again, some of those moments were the same play call, and it worked on one down and didn't work on the other. That usually goes back to some execution or a little bit different looks here and there. We've got to be better in some of those moments, and some of the play style and what we were trying to do. Ohio State has a really good defense as well. So I think our answers on third down — we spent a lot of time on third-and-long this past week with our offense, and we were able to take advantage of it because of that time that we put in."

Q: "Want to ask you about the touchdown right before half and why that was the right moment for that particular look, and then also Jamari as a ball carrier. Why was that a good fit?"

DL: "Obviously we've done some of the gate stuff in the past. That's a play that we've worked with our field goal unit since fall camp, and we knew we were going to utilize it as a gate play, so we put that in with our offense several weeks ago, and felt like that was a play that was going to be successful. It had a couple different options. You also have the ability to burn the timeout if you don't like the look right there, and you can take points. But we liked the look that we saw. He had taken snaps and done that QB sneak 50 times, at least, since August. Not necessarily with that exact same formation or the exact same personnel on the field, but several times the last few weeks, and our history against Ohio State, we've run gate against them multiple times, so we anticipated them trying to defend some of those different looks that we give them. We'd run outside runs. We'd done some different looks, but we hadn't done that, so we felt like there was a great chance it was going to be there and be available. When we saw the look, we knew it was going to be positive, and that's kind of our game on the line play from the 2-yard line and the 1-yard line, and it fit. It felt like that was a great time to take that chance and that opportunity."

Q: "The worry Saturday was if it was something serious for Teitum. Do you have an update there, and what can you say about what he means to the program?"

DL: "Teitum has been unbelievable for us this year, and every year that he's been here. Just watching him grow as a player and a person has been a lot of fun for us. But unfortunately, Teitum's done for the year. He had a knee injury. He'll end up having surgery. He's gonna have to wait for a little bit to let things settle down. I hate it for him, because it's kind of a routine, weird play that it happened on. He obviously was a huge impact in that game. You look at the fake punt and the impact that he's had on our team throughout the year. Normally I'd wait till Wednesday to talk about that, but probably not fair to him. So we'll see him walking around on crutches, and he left it on the line there on the field, man. I don't know if he'll get another chance to play as an Oregon football player, but whoever gets to have that guy on their team in the future is going to be really, really lucky."

Q: "You mentioned the struggles that Michigan is going through offensively. I feel like a lot of teams have dealt with some challenges, especially on the offensive side. You mentioned post-game where you guys were just two weeks ago, and the changes that you guys have made, the growth that you've made. I feel like those challenges for teams have created more parity across the board. What do you attribute the parity in college football to this season?"

DL: "I'm not sure what you're saying. Are you saying the coordinator changes have created the parity or what?"

Q: "I'm asking what you can attribute to the parity, because I feel like we always talk about how the college football season has a lot of parity in it, but I feel like this season we've seen more parity than usual. I'm curious if you have that same perspective and what you attribute the parity to."

DL: "I mean, 10 years ago, some of the best teams in college football had great players stacked, and there wasn't the opportunity for those players necessarily to go somewhere else. Now I think with NIL and some of the things that happen with the portal, there are a lot of transactions that happen each season, and guys that are good players aren't necessarily stacked in depth behind other good players on rosters. That's hard. We're fortunate to have a really good roster here, but there's transition every year, and I think what you see is more guys that would have been a really good two here, now they go somewhere else and they become a one, and then they develop and grow as a player, and they become really good players. I think that part of it is the distribution of talent is higher now than it's ever been. I think that's definitely one piece of the parity. The reality of playing in the conference that we're in is it looks a lot different than it did five years ago, 10 years ago. This is a really challenging conference. There are other challenging conferences in college football; they're big, and every week it's a talented team that you're playing against that has good coaches, and they have good players, and that makes it a real challenge."

Q: "You guys have had to prep for multiple quarterbacks before, but what makes (Michigan's) two quarterbacks different?"

DL: "Yeah, there are some things that are similar, and then some things that are different. Obviously, more recently, I think if you look at it, it's about who's protecting the ball better. Bryce, the strength of his arm and as a running threat is unique, but they both operate similarly. The offense (doesn't) completely change based on which guy's in the game, right? There's still some similarities in what they do now. Will it change now moving forward? That's where we have to go back and evaluate some of our Utah games. Coach Harding's been with coach Whittingham for a long, long time, so I think there's going to be some high-identity plays that probably show up based on what he's done in his history. You've got to evaluate our games. They also have a coach on staff there that's going to have some involvement, that's been at Syracuse, so you go back and look at that. But when you look at the quarterbacks, there's some similar pieces to what they both do. Just some small variances and differences."

Q: "J-Mac played a little bit in this game. What have you seen from him more as a person than as a player over these past two weeks as he's battled back from the injury and tried to get back to the player he was before going down?"

DL: "Yeah, I mean, just unbelievable resilience to return as fast as he could. It's always hard to level expectations because he wanted more than anything to be in as much as he could. He worked really, really hard to put himself in a position to get back, but I knew early in the week, like, 'Hey man, we need you not just for one, we need you for several.' So this could be — this is a build-up process, and you don't go from not playing any football at all to going to play at a really high level for a lot of snaps. When he was in there, he did a really good job. Sometimes he's open. I wish we could have been able to find him, but I think his leadership continues to show up. His work ethic continues to show up, and obviously he's a big piece of our offense and a dynamic piece. So, excited to have him back out there."

Q: "Obviously, you don't replace someone like Teitum with one player. Nasir (Wyatt) is a name that will come up. But is there anybody else? What's the plan for working without Teitum?"

DL: "I wouldn't necessarily share everybody that's going to be involved in that, but obviously Nas will step up. He's a guy that's been out there for us already, but there will be some moving parts. It'll look a little bit different. There's already been a rotation along our defensive line, so I think you'll see a lot of the familiar faces. But you don't just replace a guy like Teitum Tuioti and his experience and what he's been able to do."

Q: "Obviously, a 24-team playoff became official today. Just your thoughts on it in this moment, and then speaking to the parity that you were talking about earlier, do you feel like that parity might make a good argument for an expanded playoff?"

DL: "Yeah, not a lot of new thoughts. I mean, I think this is something the coaches have known is coming down the wire here for a little bit, so no new thoughts really on it. I do think that it's getting closer and closer to a normal playoff model in other sports, where the challenge is — we're certainly not the same team we were when we started the season, right? We've experienced some adversity, we've seen some different players on the field, we've gone through some coaching transition, but if the goal is to be able to get teams that are capable of winning at the end, I think that it allows a team like ourselves, where you can say, 'OK, the best team could be in there potentially and have a chance to go compete.' So I think you'll see some more of that. We saw it last year with Miami; they experienced a couple of losses, and they started playing their best football toward the end of the season and got all the way to the national championship. So it's gonna provide some unique opportunities. The questions about who's in, who's not in, that's just gonna exist now at a higher level of who's 20, who's 25, who's 26, who's 27. Every time the mark moves, that's always the conversation, and that'll happen again. But certainly there'll be some really quality teams playing, and obviously the loss of the conference championship games is going to be unique and sad in some respects because that's always a really awesome game to be a part of. But in reality, it's almost a punishment for those teams that are playing in it because they're playing football when nobody else is. So it certainly makes sense with the landscape of college football and what it's like right now."

Q: "Before Kyle got to Michigan, there was a lot going on in that program. You said that you've known him for a few years, gone against him before. How have you seen him handle everything that's going on this year and the ups and downs of this year and help that program get back to level ground?"

DL: "I haven't really been able to pay much attention to him until this week. So, I don't know. I know he's a Hall of Fame coach for a reason, and he's won a lot of football games. I've been worried about my own problems, not really paying attention to his. I know he does a great job. I'm sure they'll be prepared to play us."

Q: "You touched on it, just the removal of the conference championship. Do you feel that this is the right move to remove conference championships?"

DL: "I think it's a necessary evil. Like I said, I like that game. I would love for it to be a part, but I don't think it's fair necessarily to the teams. We experienced it a couple years ago. We're playing a conference championship, and everybody else is able to relax on their couch, and then we go almost a month without. I think the thing that I've always said is the game should be played in sequence, very similar to the NFL playoffs or any other playoff model. So there's still a lot to college football. I think it has to get better, but I do think if you're going to expand the games to 24 teams, then that's going to be part of what is missing."

Q: "Does Michigan's change at offensive coordinator change much for how you prepare for their offense?"

DL: "Yeah, it just makes you do a little bit of a deeper dive. Like I said, when you're trying to look to say, 'OK, what else could they pull out?' I think you know one thing you recognize about changes in college football is teams that have done that, experienced that recently, they've kind of had a resurgence on offense. I mean, whether it's a coaching change, there are several programs. I showed that to our players today. Here are programs that made changes at head coach or coordinator this season, and here's what the next week looked like or the next two weeks looked like. We've seen a lot of those teams have a lot of success. Sometimes that's not just because of a change. But there's a spark that's sometimes lit when those things happen. So we anticipate seeing their absolute best, and then we're going to have to chase ghosts a little bit and look for every answer that we might be able to find based on what might be different."

Q: "Just wondering if you could speak to the offensive line development and the sort of consistency that you've seen. Obviously, the continuity is there, but this last week in particular felt like a kind of even bigger breakthrough for that group."

DL: "Yeah, we've always felt games like that one, the rushing battle is really important. The way they're able to protect the quarterback, I think that's one of the glaring differences in that game. I know there was some chunk yardage at the end of the game that was a little different because of how we were playing defense, but ultimately, I think they rushed for like 54 yards, and we were over 100, and I think that speaks to our offense. That's a really hard front to be able to run on. We were able to protect the quarterback, and again, some of that's scheme variance, and then some of it's the way we call the game. To be able to build screens off of some of their pressures, and so all those things allow the O-line to be able to shine and have a lot of success. So I think all those things come together, and then those guys having continuity playing together, building more confidence in the calls that you're making with the guy next to you, like that, that's going to create a rhythm and allow them to perform."

Q: "I'm curious because the matchup with Michigan and what they have on that front, how is that a measuring stick? We talk about the continuity, a couple good performances, but this is a really tough group right here."

DL: "Yeah, it's as good up front as we've seen, right? There's a lot of NFL players on that defense in general, but this group, they do an unbelievable job, and it's a pressure-oriented group, from a standpoint of they're going to give you a lot. They pitch a lot of different looks. (Michigan defensive coordinator Jay Hill) has done an unbelievable job there of creating some real disruption and havoc with what they do up front, and then they play tight coverage in the back end. So there's a reason that they've had so much success defensively. It'll be a real challenge for our offensive line."

Q: "Your defense has at this point the lowest rate of missed tackles in the country. To get to that point from where you guys were at Oklahoma State, what do you attribute that to?"

Q: "I'm not sure, but probably not in that range."

DL: "Get better. Growth, right? Just a lot of work, a lot of practice. Guys taking it seriously on how they have to attack and improve. And look, that's just a sample of the previous games, right? This next game's a separate indicator, so we have to tackle well again. I know all that said, I saw some missed tackles this last game for us, so we can continue to get better there."

articles.title: Wrexham's Championship season so far: Injuries, noise & big scalps
articles.summary: Wrexham have had a slow start to the season and some off-field turbulence but having steadied the ship could they be on track for the play-offs?
articles.body:
With 15 games of the Championship season gone, Wrexham have steadied the ship.

Phil Parkinson's side responded to a run of three defeats in four matches by claiming four points from their home double header with promotion-hopefuls Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

It ensured they entered the final international window of 2026 in positive spirits.

As the club action takes a two-week break, BBC Sport Wales looks at the highs and lows of the Red Dragons' season to date.

So how does Wrexham's performance so far this term compare to the same stage last season?

Wrexham's performances in the draws with Cardiff City and Watford early on were encouraging.

They made light work of dispatching strugglers Preston North End and have earned highly-impressive wins against top sides including Millwall, Southampton and Middlesbrough.

Defensively, Wrexham's expected goals (xG) faced of 18.17 is the fourth-best in the division.

They have also made just one error leading to a goal, the joint-best return alongside four other teams in the Championship.

Up front, Kieffer Moore - who scored 13 times for the Red Dragons in all competitions last season - has netted five goals so far this term, in addition to claiming two assists.

The Wales international's return comes from an xG figure of just 3.23, meaning he has outperformed his xG by 1.77. He has also won 68 aerial duels, with only four players in the league managing more.

Others such as Jacques Ekomie, Issa Kabore, Ben Whiteman, Joe Worrall and Callum O'Hare have shown real glimpses of settling in after joining on permanent deals in the summer.

Amid the increasing noise surrounding the club's struggles earlier on, Parkinson yet again demonstrated an impressive ability to remain grounded and get his side back on track.

In terms of the league standings, Wrexham sit six points adrift of the Championship play-off places and eight clear of the relegation zone.

So there is plenty of reason for the Wrexham faithful to remain optimistic.

A shock departure and key results - inside Wrexham's seismic week

Wrexham owners' presence uplifting - Parkinson

When it comes to the numbers, only five teams have a lower xG total than Wrexham's figure of 16.80, while only three sides have managed fewer than their 50 shots on target.

Wrexham's four through balls made is - alongside Lincoln City - the joint-lowest in the division.

Home defeats by Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion were particularly underwhelming, while the 6-0 thrashing at West Ham United represented a real low point.

Following the 2-0 loss to Blackburn Rovers in October , former Wales international Nathan Blake suggested Wrexham were losing their "fear factor" and that they were in danger of becoming "ordinary".

The Red Dragons then produced a lacklustre display as they were beaten 1-0 by Sheffield United.

It promoted a strong response from Parkinson who said he and his players would not shy away from any criticism.

After the draw with Wolves, midfielder Lewis O'Brien said of the post-Blades debrief: "I think we had to look at ourselves, deep down. It was a tough couple of days."

On the back of the 1-1 draw with Wolves , which came three days after an impressive 2-0 win over Boro, Parkinson declared his side had needed a reboot following the defeat by the Blades.

"We've had a bit of a reset this week in terms of what the performances need to look like for our supporters and everybody at the club," said the manager.

"We know we've got the capabilities to win games, but like everybody, you can easily have a capability to lose a game and you've got to be right at it.

"There's no 80% scenario in this division, everybody's got to be at it, focused and ready, and we really were ready in these two games. We can take a lot of credit from that."

Injuries certainly have not helped the club's cause, while there have been several off-the-field issues too.

The Red Dragons have been fined twice fielding ineligible players.

Chief executive officer Michael Williamson departed last week, with Shaun Harvey taking over as acting CEO.

It has clearly impacted the club's efforts in the opening third of the season.

"You always have things going on in football clubs, it's never smooth running anywhere," Parkinson said after the Wolves draw.

"But I think this has been particularly disjointed, for various reasons."

Ben Sheaf, Max Cleworth and George Thomason have all returned to action in recent weeks following significant spells on the sidelines through injury.

Nathan Broadhead is also closing in on a return, although it remains to be seen when last season's top scorer Josh Windass, Callum O'Hare and Liberato Cacace will be available.

Discussing the November international window, Parkinson said: "It's a chance to get some work in the lads who need to work and build on what we've done this week."

Unfortunately, Sam Smith is set to miss the remainder of the season and will undergo surgery this week after sustaining a serious knee injury at Sheffield United.

It will likely prompt the Red Dragons to scour the transfer market for an additional frontman in January given that Bailey Cadamarteri is the only other option behind first choice striker Moore.

Davis Keillor-Dunn could also potentially be recalled from his season-long loan spell at League One side Sheffield Wednesday - where he has scored five times in 11 appearances.

But the outlook on the campaign overall has certainly improved in the past week.

Wrexham fans hope more progress can be made over the coming months.

articles.title: Vinicius y Endrick, a Singapur
articles.standfirst: 'Al otro lado del espejo', una opinión de Alfredo Relaño
articles.summary: 'Al otro lado del espejo', una opinión de Alfredo Relaño
articles.body: Brasil disputa en esta ventana FIFA dos partidos en Singapur, uno con Japón el sábado, el otro el martes con la propia Singapur. En otras condiciones supondría un palo para el Madrid, y de hecho lo es para el Barça, porque ese zarandeo se lo va a comer también Raphinha, pero en lo que se refiere a los blancos es lo contrario. Mourinho incluso dijo que agradecería a Ancelotti que diera minutos a Vinicius y Endrick porque ambos los necesitan. Más incluso Vinicius que Endrick, porque este aún está en cuarto creciente y dispuesto a pasar una inevitable travesía de banquillo dado el nivel del equipo en que milita. Pero lo de Vinicius es otra cosa. Por decirlo deprisa y bien, su mala cabeza le tiene donde está. Una suspensión de cuatro partidos ha servido para que la afición le haya colocado decididamente en condición de prescindible. Diomande ataca muy bien, defiende como el que más y no monta líos. Las dos segundas condiciones nunca las cumplió Vinicius, la primera sí, y con creces, pero hace tiempo que hace demasiado tiempo que no se le ve un gran partido. En su ausencia, el Madrid ha despegado y no por casualidad. Ahora sólo Mbappé vive desentendido del esfuerzo colectivo de recuperación, y uno se puede soportar, aunque sea a duras penas, siempre que pise la frontera del gol por partido. Pero dos ya son demasiado. Para estos asuntos, dos son más del doble que uno, porque el desajuste empieza a ser irremediable y más si algún otro que puede considerarse con el mismo derecho, léase Bellingham, cae en la tentación de permitirse lo mismo. Así que ahora Vinicius está en una posición de la que solo puede sacarse él mismo. Mourinho no querrá enterrarle, sería absurdo, pero tampoco sería prudente averiar el funcionamiento que ha alcanzado haciéndole pasar ahora por delante de un jugador que está cubriendo la posición con notable alto, y que por su juventud está llamado a mejorar. De ahí que le pida Ancelotti minutos para Vinicius, de ahí que, por una vez, de estos secuestros de jugadores para maniobras de provecho económico de chupópteros anónimos resulte algo de provecho.

articles.title: Ya era hora, Raúl entrenador
articles.standfirst: Una opinión de Roberto Gómez
articles.summary: Una opinión de Roberto Gómez
articles.body: Raúl González Blanco, sin duda el mejor jugador español que ha vestido la camiseta del Real Madrid y leyenda con el 7 a la espalda de la selección española, coge las riendas del Real Oviedo. Raúl pertenece al grupo de leyendas blancas como Míchel, Fernando Hierro o Rafa Martín Vázquez están preparados pasa asumir el reto de dirigir a un equipo y, aunque están en el mercado pero no entrenan. Ése ya no es el caso del que fuera 7 blanco. Raúl demostró en el Castilla el grandísimo entrenador que es, y lo normal y lógico habría sido que llegara a ser técnico del primer equipo. Pero ese paso finalmente no se dio. Raúl está más que preparado. Tiene ilusión, conocimiento y muchísimas ganas de entrenar. Es una alegría para el Real Oviedo y para la Segunda diviisón su llegada. Tendrá la oportunidad de demostrar lo que es como entrenador. Y será beneficioso para el Oviedo pues Raúl es una marca pero que muy importante en la historia del fútbol mundial . Habrá muchos, por no decir muchísimos, que desearan que fracase. Una pena. Porque Raúl siempre, dentro y fuera del campo, ha demostrado su amor por el fútbol. Ahora como técnico Del Real Oviedo le deseamos que tenga toda la suerte del mundo y seguro que más de uno en breve se arrepentirá de no haber contratado al 7 de España. Raúl González blanco. Bien negociadas por Karanka y Luis de la Fuente las ausencias de Lamine y Oyarzabal para el partido de España frente a la República Checa que entrena Santi Denia. Médicos, clubes, entrenadores y la selección están de acuerdo en que lo primero es el estado físico de los jugadores y seguro que en el partido frente a Inglaterra ambos estarán. Fran Soto está contento con la comparecencia de los árbitros tras los partidos de Primera. Para el Comité, los colegiados estuvieron perfectos hasta el punto que se había previsto la posibilidad de darles instrucciones de lo que tenían que hablar y, de momento, no hay necesidad de hacerlo. Libertad total.

articles.title: El Barça toca madera
articles.standfirst: Confía en que ninguno de sus jugadores regrese lesionado del parón de selecciones
articles.summary: Confía en que ninguno de sus jugadores regrese lesionado del parón de selecciones
articles.body: El Barcelona afronta a partir de este lunes un nuevo parón de selecciones, el último de este año 2026. Y siempre que se produce la llamada de las selecciones, existe temor en el club por cómo volverán los jugadores. Motivos no faltan. Solo hay que echar un vistazo a cómo han regresado algunos de sus futbolistas, que han sufrido importantes lesiones durante sus compromisos internacionales. Hay dos casos que preocupan especialmente. Uno de ellos es Raphinha. El brasileño ha regresado lesionado de las tres últimas convocatorias con su selección. La primera vez fue en el último parón de la temporada 2025/26, una lesión que le impidió estar a buen nivel en el tramo final de la campaña. Posteriormente, llegó la lesión durante el Mundial y, por último, sufrió un nuevo percance en el último parón. El jugador ha recibido el aviso del cuerpo técnico azulgrana de que debe tener cuidado para evitar una nueva lesión. No puede arriesgar en absoluto, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que los partidos que disputa son amistosos. Raphinha lo tiene claro y ya ha hablado con Ancelotti. "Sabe que tiene que repartir minutos. Para la selección también sería complicado que sufriera una lesión. Hemos hablado y sabe que me estoy recuperando de la última dolencia. Estoy bien, pero no al cien por cien. Que los culés no estén preocupados, porque me cuido mucho", dijo Raphinha la semana pasada durante el acto de renovación con el Barcelona. Otro jugador que ha regresado lesionado después de una convocatoria con su selección ha sido Frenkie de Jong. La última vez fue durante el pasado Mundial, cuando volvió con una importante lesión de ligamentos. El jugador recibió numerosas críticas por no haber parado a tiempo en Estados Unidos y también por no acudir rápidamente a Barcelona para someterse a una revisión médica. El resultado fue que el neerlandés estuvo cerca de cuatro meses sin poder jugar. Reapareció hace unos días y ha rendido a buen nivel, demostrando que está plenamente recuperado. De hecho, fue uno de los jugadores clave en el partido del pasado domingo frente al Atlético de Madrid. Flick no quiere que vuelva a sufrir un percance físico. Para evitar problemas, la prevención es fundamental. No hay que asumir riesgos cuando aparecen pequeñas molestias. Este es el caso de Lamine Yamal, que no disputará el partido frente a la República Checa debido a unas molestias en la rodilla. Se recuperará durante unos días en Barcelona y, si evoluciona favorablemente, podrá jugar el siguiente encuentro frente a Inglaterra.

articles.title: Michael Carrick está condenado en el Manchester United y Pochettino se suma a la lista de candidatos
articles.standfirst: Eddie Howe, Jyulian Nagelsmann, Antonio Conte y Mauricio Pochettino son los cuatro principales candidatos a sustituir a Michael Carrick
articles.summary: Eddie Howe, Jyulian Nagelsmann, Antonio Conte y Mauricio Pochettino son los cuatro principales candidatos a sustituir a Michael Carrick
articles.body: El Manchester United ya ha tomado una decisión definitiva sobre el futuro de Michael Carrick, y según adelanta 'The Athletic' el técnico dejará el banquillo de 'Old Trafford'. El director ejecutivo, Omar Berrada, y el director de fútbol, Jason Wilcox, recomendarán al copropietario Sir Jim Ratcliffe y a la familia Glazer la destitución de Carrick, aprovechando el parón de selecciones para buscar un sustituto. La directiva del United consideró destituir a Carrick tras la derrota ante el Bournemouth, pero finalmente decidió que el inglés merecía la oportunidad de demostrar que podía revertir la situación. El empate 4-4 frente al Aston Villa supone que el United actualmente decimoctavo en la clasificación de la Premie League, ha protagonizado su peor inicio de temporada en una competición nacional en los últimos 40 años. Solo el Crystal Palace y el Ipswich han recibido más goles que los 19 que ha encajado el United en la Premier League esta temporada. Eddie Howe (Newcastle), Jyulian Nagelsmann, Antonio Conte y Mauricio Pochettino (que renovó como seleccionador de Estados Unidos hasta 2030) son los cuatro principales candidatos a sustituir a Michael Carrick en el Manchester United tras las calabazas de Didier Deschamps.

articles.title: El dilema del Sevilla con Fofana
articles.standfirst: En Nervión se abre un debate sobre la posición que más puede beneficiar al centrocampista francés
articles.summary: En Nervión se abre un debate sobre la posición que más puede beneficiar al centrocampista francés
articles.body: El bache de resultados que atraviesa el Sevilla puede explicarse en gran parte por el bajón de rendimiento de Youssouf Fofana, uno de los fichajes más destacados esta temporada y el que ha acaparado casi todos los focos. Por este motivo, en los últimos días se ha alimentado el debate sobre cuál es la demarcación ideal para el futbolista francés. Un asunto capital en el equipo hispalense, que necesita recuperar cuanto antes la mejor versión de su pieza más diferencial. Hasta el momento, la realidad es que Luis García Plaza se ha mantenido fiel al mismo dibujo inicial, un 4-2-3-1 en fase ofensiva y un 4-4-2 en fase defensiva. Eso sí, ha probado diferentes variantes en zona de enganche, desde un segundo delantero (Isaac Romero) hasta centrocampistas con un perfil box to box (Jon Guridi y Fofana), además de un mediapunta más al uso como Peque. Las características del elegido son las que condicionan su rol en la posición. Por ejemplo, Isaac es el que más metros recorre a lo ancho del campo, mientras que Fofana es el que más lo hace a lo largo. "Fofana puede jugar en los dos sitios. Primero, no es un doble pivote, con todo mi respeto, es un 6 y un 8; Luci (Agoumé) sí es un mediocentro. Jugamos con un mediocentro de posición, otro más adelantado y un 10, entonces, no jugamos con dos puntas. El otro día -contra Osasuna- me gustó mucho en el mediocentro y cuando le pusimos por delante en Getafe estuvo bastante flojo", desarrolló García Plaza tras el empate frente al Alavés. Los números del Sevilla en esta Liga respaldan la presencia de Fofana partiendo desde la medular junto a Agoumé. En los seis partidos en que ambos comenzaron jugando en el centro del campo (Valencia, Deportivo, Real Madrid, Osasuna, Getafe y Alavés), los blanquirrojos consiguieron 10 puntos de 18 posibles, aunque en cuatro de ellos el jugador cedido por el Milan acabó adelantando su posición tras las sustituciones. Ante Valencia, Osasuna, Getafe y Alavés actuó justo por detrás de un segundo delantero, en este caso Isaac, con un balance de 7 de 12 puntos. Durante esta temporada, Fofana ha salido como titular en la media punta únicamente contra el Barcelona y el Levante. Si bien es cierto que en esos dos encuentros el galo aportó un gol y una asistencia, el Sevilla apenas pudo rascar un punto. Una de las principales virtudes de Fofana es su potencia para romper líneas con la pelota en los pies. En sus nueve apariciones ha realizado 54 conducciones con las que ha recorrido 713,1 metros, sobresaliendo especialmente sus 40 carreras progresivas. Cada vez que avanza con el esférico promedia 13.2 metros por conducción, una estadística donde solo le supera Chidera Ejuke (13.4). Ahora acumula dos jornadas consecutivas en las que no explota esta faceta, algo que le ayudaba al Sevilla a generar desajustes en los rivales. El freno parcial de Fofana también ha reducido su influencia cerca del área contraria. En el plano creativo exhibe una notable fiabilidad con un 83.3% de acierto en pases en jugadas a campo abierto y un 76.5% en el último tercio, siendo el tercero mejor del Sevilla en ambos registros. Esta buena visión le ha llevado a ser actualmente el máximo asistente de los nervionenses con tres pases de gol. Sin embargo, ante Getafe y Alavés completó una media de 18 pases, cuando en los seis choques anteriores se fue hasta más de 25. A diferencia de lo que podría pensarse cuando llegó al Sevilla, Fofana ha demostrado que posee más capacidad en fase ofensiva que defensiva. Y es que, pese a su enorme trabajo en la presión, sus porcentajes de duelos son discretos: un 46.9% de éxito en los terrestres y un 42.9% en los aéreos, quedándose fuera del top 10 de la plantilla en ambos aspectos. Es decir, tal como argumentó Luis García Plaza, está lejos de ser un mediocentro posicional, y justo ahí reside el dilema. Cuando Fofana juega como centrocampista ayuda a equilibrar a Agoumé, una labor para la que quizás existen alternativas más eficaces como Kochorashvili y que le resta llegada al área rival. Por el contrario, si adelanta su demarcación, su despliegue físico mejora la presión alta, pero su fútbol se vuelve más previsible ante defensas cerradas que conceden menos espacios para correr, además de privar a Isaac Romero del contexto que más le favorece. "Lleva dos partidos en que no ha estado tan bien. Cuando uno se acostumbra a que un jugador esté al nivel que estaba él… pero confiamos en él y va a recuperar ese nivel", expresó García Plaza respecto a Fofana. Una las grandes tareas del técnico madrileño durante el parón será averiguar cómo exprimir al máximo las cualidades del futbolista con mayor calidad del equipo, ya sea mediante su posición o el panorama que lo rodea.

articles.title: Miroslav Klose: FC Nuremberg boss on strikers, Harry Kane and coaching
articles.summary: Miroslav Klose rose from amateur to World Cup winner as a player - now the German is forging a similar path as a coach.
articles.body:
It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.

He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.

But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.

"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.

"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.

"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.

"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."

That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?

"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."

Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.

It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.

Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.

He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.

Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.

The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.

"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner .

"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.

"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.

"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."

Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.

"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.

"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."

Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.

He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.

This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.

"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.

"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.

"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.

"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.

"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."

Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.

"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.

"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.

"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."

Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.

"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.

"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."

So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?

"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.

"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.

"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

articles.title: Raúl Varela: "Al fútbol español le hacen falta muchos Raúles en los banquillos"
articles.standfirst: El director de La Tribu aplaude la nueva etapa del exfutbolista del Real Madrid y recuerda las oportunidades que nunca llegaron para dirigir al primer equipo blanco
articles.summary: El director de La Tribu aplaude la nueva etapa del exfutbolista del Real Madrid y recuerda las oportunidades que nunca llegaron para dirigir al primer equipo blanco
articles.body: La llegada de Raúl González Blanco al banquillo del Real Oviedo ha sido una de las grandes noticias de la actualidad futbolística. Después de su etapa en la cantera del Real Madrid, el exdelantero madridista afronta una nueva aventura en los banquillos. Una oportunidad que Raúl Varela ha celebrado en su editorial de La Tribu de Radio MARCA, donde también ha reflexionado sobre las dificultades que supone para un entrenador dar el salto a un nuevo proyecto cuando entran en juego las circunstancias familiares. "¿O nos vamos todos o me quedo en casa?", comenzó Varela, recordando la historia de otro entrenador, una leyenda del fútbol español, que estuvo cerca de aceptar una importante oferta de un club europeo. Una negociación que incluía tres años de contrato, una propuesta económica importante y plena confianza, pero que terminó frustrándose por una cuestión familiar. "Los niños dijeron que le daban igual los Avios de la Iberia Plus y que se quedaban y la operación se frustró hasta nuevo aviso", explicó. Una situación que el periodista relacionó con la trayectoria reciente de Raúl González. "Algo parecido, dicen los que le conocen de cerca y que no son muchos, le ha ocurrido a Raúl González Blanco, digan lo que digan, leyenda máxima de nuestro fútbol y que aspira a serlo también en los banquillos", aseguró. Varela también repasó el paso de Raúl por la cantera madridista, donde desarrolló buena parte de su trayectoria como entrenador. El periodista destacó su "trabajo bien ponderado y con frutos evidentes en Valdebebas donde echó raíces como nadie en el Castilla". Sin embargo, su nombre nunca terminó de convertirse en una apuesta definitiva para el banquillo del primer equipo. "Su nombre se asoció en un par de ocasiones al primer equipo, pero entre Ancelotti, Alonso, Arbeloa y ahora Mourinho el 'suena Raúl', versión moderna del 'suena Míchel' de antaño acabó por convertirse en una especie de maldición", señaló Varela. Una situación que terminó llevando al exfutbolista a abandonar el club blanco y esperar una oportunidad que encajase con sus prioridades personales. Según explicó el periodista, Raúl decidió salir del Real Madrid "dispuesto a vivir la vida familiar que siempre ha antepuesto esperando que el teléfono sonase con la oferta adecuada". Esa llamada finalmente llegó desde Asturias. "Y llegó. En Oviedo. En el Tartiere", celebró Varela, aunque también mostró su desacuerdo con la destitución de Julián Calero, al que definió como "un entrenador reputado y de solvencia". El periodista se mostró convencido de lo que puede aportar el exmadridista al conjunto asturiano. "Aparece Raúl para sublimar el talento y exigir entrega incondicional y que los carbayones se sientan orgullosos de su equipo y, a ser posible, brindando con un culín de sidra por el retorno a primera división", afirmó. Varela cerró su editorial con una defensa de la presencia de figuras como Raúl en el fútbol nacional. "Es una gran noticia. Al fútbol español le hacen falta muchos Raúles en los banquillos y en la primera plana de actualidad", concluyó.

articles.title: James Penrice: Scotland and Rangers defender on his 'slow rise' from part-time football to international call-up
articles.summary: The 27-year-old defender has been handed his first Scotland call-up by Sebastien Pocognoli; Penrice is on loan at Rangers with an option to buy; Scotland host North Macedonia on November 13, with their final Nations League game away to Switzerland three days later
articles.body:
James Penrice is the first to admit he has made a "slow rise" in football after an "unbelievable" few months resulted in his first Scotland call-up at the age of 27.

He scored on his Rangers debut a day after joining on loan from AEK Athens, and has continued to be a key player for Derek McInnes' side.

"I knew coming back and obviously playing for Rangers there's always going to be a chance in the Scotland squad," he told Sky Sports News.

"It was one of my decisions to come back to try and push. Ultimately, I came back to play for Rangers but it's an added bonus to manage to get the call-up as well. It's been unbelievable since I came back."

The Greek club paid £2m for the defender after an impressive season at Hearts. He went on to play 32 times as the side secured another national title.

Penrice's career started at Partick Thistle, with loan spells at East Fife and Livingston before a permanent move to the West Lothian club.

"It's kind of been a slow rise, don't get me wrong," he added.

"When we [Partick Thistle] dropped down to League One there was part of me that thought I was done.

"I'd been part-time and, especially when Covid hit, I was looking at courses and stuff like that and trying to think about life after football.

"From then, I got my head down and then I went to Livingston and that was kind of the super bolt.

"Davey Martindale [the Livi manager] said that it was kind of the last chance I had for full-time football and I grasped it there.

"The move to Hearts was a good personal season for me. Then obviously I moved to Greece, so it's been a bit mental from where I was at 20. It makes it more interesting, doesn't it!"

Penrice might be a new face in the latest Scotland squad, but he will also be one of the older players.

He insists he is proof that you need to break into the international set-up in the early years of your career to be a success.

"I think you see nowadays that there's 17, 18-year-olds winning World Cups, and I think boys when they get to 21 or 22 they think their career's done.

"I was in League One at 23, so it's all about putting your head down and hard work. Don't get me wrong you need luck, you can create your own luck.

"Hard work and just really sticking at it and believing in yourself and you've always got a chance.

The loan to Rangers includes an option to buy, with McInnes already stressing his desire to keep the defender on a permanent deal.

"I think the good thing for us is that you want all parties to be willing to try and make it happen," the Ibrox boss said.

"I want him, the club wants him and James wants to be here. From that starting point, hopefully we can get something agreed.

"When and how that can be delivered, I don't know yet. We've still got work to do and I'll leave that to the people upstairs. But, James has made it clear how keen he is to stay.

"Bringing him here was important for me. He plays with hunger, he's desperate to be a successful Rangers player and I think he shows that in his performances."

articles.title: La revaloración de Prestianni 266 días de su 'Vinicius Gate': cuesta 100 millones y lo quieren los grandes
articles.standfirst: PSG y Bayern de Múnich tienen al joven futbolista argentino del Benfica en su lista de prioridades
articles.summary: PSG y Bayern de Múnich tienen al joven futbolista argentino del Benfica en su lista de prioridades
articles.body: Gianluca Prestianni, el jugador argentino al que Vinicius acusó de llamarle "mono" el 17 de febrero de 2026 y que fue el causante de la denominada 'Ley Vinicius', ve como su carrera se revaloriza más de 10 meses después de su incidente con el brasileño. La 'Ley Vinicius', que provocó Prestianni (aunque él negó los insultos), castiga con expulsión a cualquier futbolista que se cubra la boca con la mano, la camiseta o cualquier otro objeto mientras discute o se encara con un rival o con el árbitro. El objetivo es evitar que los jugadores oculten insultos, provocaciones verbales o comentarios racistas. Gianluca Prestianni, que apenas tiene 20 años y firmó con el Benfica hasta 2029, despunta este curso con 12 goles y 6 asistencias en 20 partidos. Pedro Sousa, comentarista de 'Now', prevé una venta del argentino Prestianni (1,66 m.) al final de la temporada por una cantidad que rondará los 100 millones de euros. "Veo al PSG presionando al Benfica en enero, y el Bayern ha estado siguiendo al jugador", adelantó en el programa 'Record na Hora'.
